doc.title: Mickey Roker interviewed by Michael Woods, Majesty of the Seas, May 31, 1995

title: Gillespie's Afro-Cuban rhythms and what he taught
summary: Gillespie loved Chano Pozo and other conga players and taught Roker six-eight and Latin beats that infiltrated jazz.

story.theme_name: Charlie Parker, Dizzy and the bebop revolution
story.community_name: Charlie Parker: encounters, lore and legacy

blocks.x: Now I want to ask you about, pertaining to Dizzy, and then you kind of plug me in to it as a drummer. You know Dizzy was influential in bringing the Afro-Cuban beats into the © Fillius Jazz Archive -4-
bebop and into other styles. And that’s something that, you know, you’re a specialist in. You’re pretty good at that.
Well I do the best I can.
Tell us about how that affects the sound and how that changes the style.

Well he loves rhythm. He loves rhythm, you know what I mean? He’s like the king of bebop you know what I’m saying? He’s like “titty boom, titty boom” so he fell in love with Chano Pozo and Patato Valdez, you know and Big Black, I mean these are great conga players. And he just loves that kind of music. And for me it was beautiful man because he taught me some rhythms — he taught me six-eight rhythms, and different Latin beats, but he loved six-eight rhythm, that are so simple, but still complicated you know? If he don’t show you, it’s even hard to conceive of these rhythms. And it’s hard for me to express because I had to learn it from him you know. But he’s a great man, Dizzy Gillespie, he’s knows everything about music. And he just loved, you know, the Afro-Cuban beat you know. And it infiltrated into jazz you know.
